title: Module 4: Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & Go-to-Market
description: Plan the lifecycle of an AI feature: define scope, set expectations, align stakeholders, manage change, and measure success with KPIs.

questions.question: When planning an AI feature's lifecycle, what should be the first step before any technical design?
options: Build a proof of concept immediately
Define the problem scope, success criteria, and stakeholder expectations in writing
Choose the largest Claude model available
Write the system prompt first
questions.explanation: Before any technical design, architects must define the problem scope, success metrics, and stakeholder expectations to ensure the solution addresses real needs.

questions.question: What is a 'golden dataset' in the context of Claude solution development?
options: A dataset with the most expensive API calls
A curated set of representative inputs and expected outputs used for evaluation, regression testing, and quality assurance
The entire training data of Claude
A dataset used only for marketing demos
questions.explanation: A golden dataset provides a stable benchmark of representative cases with known good outputs, enabling consistent evaluation and regression testing across iterations.

questions.question: Which KPI is most important for measuring the success of a Claude-based customer support system?
options: Number of API calls per second
Customer satisfaction (CSAT), first-contact resolution rate, and escalation rate
Length of the system prompt
Total tokens consumed
questions.explanation: Business-aligned KPIs like CSAT, first-contact resolution, and escalation rates measure actual user impact rather than technical metrics alone.

questions.question: What is the recommended approach for managing stakeholder expectations during the development of a Claude-based solution?
options: Promise the best possible results to win support
Set realistic expectations about AI capabilities, limitations, and the iterative nature of development with regular demos and feedback loops
Avoid sharing progress until the final release
Tell stakeholders the system will never make mistakes
questions.explanation: Managing expectations requires honest communication about AI limitations, regular demos for feedback, and iterative improvement rather than overpromising.

questions.question: In the lifecycle of a Claude-based feature, what is the purpose of a 'staged rollout'?
options: To increase development time unnecessarily
To limit initial blast radius, gather real-world feedback, and iterate before full-scale deployment
To avoid testing entirely
To release only to internal users permanently
questions.explanation: Staged rollouts (alpha → beta → GA) limit risk by exposing the feature to progressively larger audiences, gathering feedback, and iterating before full release.

questions.question: What is the role of 'change management' when introducing Claude-based tools to an organization?
options: Change management is not needed for AI tools
Address human factors: training, communication, addressing fears about job displacement, and supporting users through the transition
Change management only applies to non-technical changes
Only IT departments need change management
questions.explanation: AI adoption requires addressing human concerns (job security, workflow changes), providing training, and communicating benefits to ensure smooth adoption.

questions.question: When defining success metrics for a Claude-based solution, what is the difference between 'leading' and 'lagging' indicators?
options: There is no difference
Leading indicators predict future outcomes (e.g., prompt quality score, test pass rate); lagging indicators measure past results (e.g., monthly revenue impact)
Leading indicators are more important than lagging ones
Lagging indicators are always more accurate
questions.explanation: Leading indicators (predictive) help steer development before problems become visible in lagging indicators (outcome-based historical metrics).

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'pre-mortem' in the planning phase of a Claude project?
options: To write an obituary for the project
To proactively identify potential failure modes and design mitigations before they occur
To celebrate project completion early
To assign blame for potential issues
questions.explanation: A pre-mortem is a planning exercise where the team imagines the project has failed and works backward to identify likely causes and design preventive measures.

questions.question: When presenting a Claude-based solution to non-technical stakeholders, what approach is most effective?
options: Explain the underlying transformer architecture in detail
Focus on business outcomes, user impact, and concrete examples rather than technical implementation details
Show only the API documentation
Avoid showing any examples
questions.explanation: Non-technical stakeholders care about business value, user impact, and ROI — not technical architecture. Concrete examples and demos bridge the gap.

questions.question: What is the 'enforcement ladder' in the context of Claude-based operational governance?
options: A ranking of employees by their Claude usage
A graduated response framework: warn, block, escalate to human, or deny based on the severity of a detected risk or violation
A list of approved Claude models
A method for increasing API throughput
questions.explanation: The enforcement ladder provides graduated governance responses, from soft warnings to hard blocks and human escalation, matching severity to action.

questions.question: In a Claude solution lifecycle, what is the purpose of a 'retrospective' after deployment?
options: To assign blame for any issues
To systematically review what worked, what didn't, and what to improve for future iterations
To celebrate success and never look at problems
To document only the positive outcomes
questions.explanation: Retrospectives capture lessons learned (both positive and negative) to improve future Claude solution development and operational practices.

questions.question: What is the recommended cadence for reviewing and updating a Claude-based solution after production deployment?
options: Never update once deployed
Regular review cycles (e.g., monthly or quarterly) to assess performance, update prompts, and incorporate feedback
Only update when the model is completely broken
Update every hour
questions.explanation: Claude-based solutions need ongoing maintenance: regular reviews to assess performance drift, update prompts, refine tools, and incorporate user feedback.

questions.question: When building a go-to-market strategy for an AI feature, what should come before the technical launch?
options: The technical launch should happen first
A communication plan, user training, support documentation, and stakeholder alignment on success criteria
No preparation is needed for AI features
Only the engineering team needs to be informed
questions.explanation: Successful GTM requires communication, training, documentation, and stakeholder buy-in before the technical launch to ensure adoption and minimize disruption.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'A/B testing' in a Claude-based solution's lifecycle?
options: To test the alphabetical order of responses
To compare two variants (e.g., different prompts, models, or workflows) on real user metrics to determine which performs better
To test only the UI design
To eliminate the need for human evaluation
questions.explanation: A/B testing with real user metrics (not just developer judgment) provides empirical evidence for which prompt, model, or workflow variant delivers better outcomes.

questions.question: In the context of a Claude solution, what does 'total cost of ownership' (TCO) include beyond API costs?
options: Only the API costs
API costs, engineering time, infrastructure, monitoring, security controls, training, and ongoing maintenance
Only the cost of Claude models
Only the cost of human reviewers
questions.explanation: TCO encompasses the full cost picture: API usage, development effort, infrastructure, observability, security, training, and ongoing maintenance over the solution's lifetime.
